transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-11 15:00 UTC / Duration 75m / Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SRE); Daniel Park (Nimbus), Rina Sato (Nimbus), Omar Rahman (Nimbus)

Summary (auto): quick hands-on deep dive on Private VPC networking patterns for Redwood Private + Dedicated, focusing on NAT hairpin egress, DNS resolution, PrivateLink endpoints, KV cache prefix routing, batching/quantization tradeoffs, and a short runtime lab checklist.

Topics: networking topology, NAT gateway vs NAT instance hairpinning, cross-account PrivateLink, DNS resolver placement, MTU and jumbo frame issues, KV cache affinity and cache warm strategies, dynamic batching, quantization performance impact on latency, pilot checklist.

Transcript:
00:00 Avery Chen: okay great thanks everyone for jumping on, um we wanted to run this as a lab style session, a little less slide heavy and more "pull your VPC config up and we can map things" — is that still the plan on your side?
00:14 Daniel Park: yes that's perfect, we have the route tables and subnets open. quick note, our VPC sits behind a transit gateway and we use cross-account PrivateLink for some downstream data services.
00:27 Priya Patel: cool, that actually helps. first thing we'll do is map the traffic egress path for inference requests — when calls go to your private redwood runtime, do they go through a nat gateway or do you have an egress proxy?
00:42 Omar Rahman: currently we have two NAT gateways in the public subnets, and egress via an outbound proxy in another account. occasionally we see hairpin issues — like callbacks to internal endpoints failing.
00:55 Priya Patel: okay hairpinning is a common gotcha. just to be clear, by hairpin you mean the scenario where an instance in a private subnet goes out to the public NAT and then back into the VPC to hit a private endpoint, right?
01:08 Omar Rahman: yeah, exactly — we suspect MTU fragmentation with jumbo frames sometimes, but also DNS resolution timing.
01:22 Liam O'Connor: silence — can I jump in? we've seen TTLs on AWS resolver endpoints cause weird stale resolution when cross-account privatelink is present. sometimes the client's resolver caches an old A record and then the traffic lands on the wrong AZ, which breaks the persistence of the KV cache affinity.
01:39 Daniel Park: kv what? (laugh) sorry, yes the K V cache affinity — we rely on sticky routing to keep the per-request cached KV state warm.
01:49 Priya Patel: thank you. so two layers: network path and runtime affinity. on the network side, if your requests get hairpinned or bounce across NATs then the source IP changes and the smart-router can't keep the KV cache hot for that session; you'll see cold cache misses and latency spikes.
02:05 Rina Sato: what's the recommended topology when you run Redwood Private in our VPC with PrivateLink endpoints in a different account?
02:17 Priya Patel: best practice we recommend is: terminate PrivateLink in a dedicated service VPC with interface endpoints, then route to the runtime subnets via AWS Transit Gateway or peering. keep egress to the internet via an egress VPC — avoid going out through a public NAT in the path between clients and the runtime. that reduces hairpin.
02:36 Avery Chen: also, if you can, use cross-account interface endpoints for control plane and data plane endpoints separately. we sometimes see control-plane DNS caching issues if both are colocated.
02:48 Omar Rahman: quick question about DNS — we have AmazonProvidedDNS in the private subnets but we also run a haproxy-based outbound proxy. how do we ensure the runtime resolves the privatelink endpoint consistently?
03:03 Priya Patel: point the runtime at your VPC resolver (172.16.0.2 style) or a forwarded resolver that knows the privatelink zones. avoid hard-coding public resolvers like 8.8.8.8 on the runtime host. also set shorter TTLs on the CNAME records you control so in failovers the resolver refreshes quickly.
03:23 Liam O'Connor: and add health checks on the interface endpoints, yes? we've seen endpoint DNS dropouts unexpectedly.
03:31 Priya Patel: yes health-checking and Route 53 failover policies are helpful. also watch out for DNS search path length — the runtime's glibc resolver will append search domains which can cause truncation.
03:45 Daniel Park: switching to KV cache and batching — curious what quantization affects. we planned to push int8 quantized weights to reduce GPU memory but worried about latency regression.
03:57 Priya Patel: quantization can reduce GPU memory and sometimes increase throughput but there are tradeoffs. on our runtime, int8 reduces kernel time for matmul but increases pre/post processing when dequantizing, so per-token latency can move either way depending on batch size and sequence length.
04:15 Marisol Vega: do you have benchmarks by sequence length? our inference tends to be short chat-like prompts, avg seq 64 tokens.
04:25 Priya Patel: for short sequences, smaller batch sizes, int8 often helps because it reduces memory pressure and allows more concurrent requests per GPU. for long sequences or use of KV cache across many tokens, the per-step dequant overhead can add up. we'll share a short table after the call.
04:42 Daniel Park: regarding KV cache warm strategy, can we pin routing to keep the same worker? we have multiple AZ spread and autoscaling.
04:53 Priya Patel: you can either use sticky affinity at the smart-router level (session cookie or source IP) or maintain a distributed prefix-KV cache with consistent hashing. stickiness is simpler but has availability tradeoffs; distributed caching requires more network east-west bandwidth and has more operational complexity.
05:15 Omar Rahman: how does this interact with autoscaling — if the worker is terminated, do you have automatic fallback to another worker with a cache-miss heavy path?
05:26 Priya Patel: yes, our runtime will fallback to a compatible model variant in another pool; you will see a cold cache warm up but we also have an optional remote KV checkpointing to S3 (or a fast redis) to speed recovery. that said it increases egress traffic.
05:42 Daniel Park: speaking of egress — our compliance team needs to log all outbound connections and we prefer to use our customer's proxy for outbound. is Redwood compatible with an explicit egress proxy?
05:54 Priya Patel: yes, we support HTTP / HTTPS proxies and we can configure the runtime to use a CONNECT style proxy for external calls. the tricky part is when the egress proxy sits in a separate account and triggers hairpin; recommended pattern is to colocate the proxy in the same AZ and keep private routing local.
06:12 Rina Sato: we have a specific constraint — the runtime must not have direct internet access, only allowed via a vetted egress proxy. does that block PrivateLink?
06:24 Priya Patel: no, PrivateLink endpoints are interface endpoints within the VPC — SDK calls to the PrivateLink address do not require going out to the internet. just ensure route tables and security groups allow the runtime to connect to the ENIs for the interface endpoints.
06:38 Avery Chen: quick aside on NLB vs ALB — for high throughput we usually recommend NLB in TCP mode to avoid premature timeouts and to preserve source IPs for affinity. ALB can be used but it terminates TLS and changes source IPs which complicates sticky routing.
06:56 Daniel Park: hmm we currently front with ALB; can we put NLB in front of the runtime privately?
07:05 Priya Patel: yes, NLB internal facing in the service VPC and then register targets via IP mode — or use target groups registered with ENIs. small nuance: NLB preserves source IP which helps KV affinity, but you need to ensure security groups don't block the source.
07:22 Omar Rahman: let's walk through a toy diagram — our request path: client -> ALB (public) -> NAT -> runtime private subnet -> privatelink -> data-store. where's the easiest swap to avoid hairpin?
07:36 Priya Patel: two options. 1) terminate ALB at the edge VPC and use an internal NLB to reach runtime, avoid NAT between ALB and runtime so no hairpin. 2) if you must keep NAT, ensure NAT doesn't change source IP (hard) — better to route through transit gateway and interface endpoints instead.
07:54 Liam O'Connor: also watch MTU. if your path crosses a transit gateway with jumbo frames disabled you can get fragmentation. runtime gRPC streams are sensitive to packet drops.
08:05 Rina Sato: are there any kernel tunables we should change on the runtime hosts?
08:12 Priya Patel: increase net.core.rmem_max and wmem_max a bit, and set tcp_mtu_probing=1 in odd MTU environments. and tune keepalive timeouts for long streaming sessions. we'll send exact recommended values.
08:26 Daniel Park: ok let's demo one runtime config — Priya do you want to show the KV cache affinity log sample?
08:32 Priya Patel: sure I'll paste a snippet. (screen share sounds) right now you can see the router decision: session id -> worker 3 -> backend 10.0.3.24:5100; that's sticky by session cookie. if you look at the cache hit metric you'll see warm starts when the same session hits the same worker.
08:50 Omar Rahman: the logs we looked at earlier showed alternating worker assignments every request. that explains the big latency variance.
08:58 Priya Patel: that suggests your source IP is changing due to NAT or the client is not preserving cookies. check the ALB settings: are sticky cookies enabled? if ALB is external and you re-proxy through NAT your source IP changes.
09:13 Daniel Park: here's an excerpt of our route table, we have a route to 0.0.0.0/0 via the nat gw and privatelink endpoints in a separate route table.
09:24 Priya Patel: ok one more quick runtime note — batching configuration: for low-latency workloads set max_batch_size small (4-8) and max_batch_wait_ms very low (10-25). we saw in your logs bursts of 64 which increases p99 latency.
09:40 Rina Sato: how about dynamic batching vs fixed? we thought dynamic helps throughput but hurts p99.
09:48 Priya Patel: dynamic batching improves throughput for asynchronous workloads. for synchronous request/response with tight p99 targets, use smaller batches and take advantage of multiple workers and quantization tradeoffs.
09:58 Daniel Park: is there a guideline for memory/per-GPU with int8 vs fp16?
10:04 Priya Patel: approximate: int8 can reduce memory by ~40% relative to fp16 depending on model and extra optimizer state. that allows 1.5-2x concurrency on the same GPU for small models. but test with your exact model because shape and attention kernels matter.
10:19 Liam O'Connor: back to DNS for a second — if we put outbound resolver in a separate account, do we need a cross-account route or endpoints?
10:28 Priya Patel: you'd set up a resolver endpoint or forwarding rules. Route 53 resolver endpoints allow inbound/outbound forwarding cross-account; you can also host a small resolver in the service VPC and forward to it. ensure security groups on the resolver allow the runtime subnet CIDRs.
10:44 Omar Rahman: operational question: how do we collect debug traces when we see KV cache thrashing?
10:50 Priya Patel: we provide a tracing hook that logs router decisions, cache hit rates, and request metadata. you can scrub PII and forward traces into your datadog/elk. for pilot we'll enable debug-level router logs for a short window.
11:05 Daniel Park: we have compliance: everything egressed must go through our proxy and must be audited. how does Redwood produce audit logs for model calls?
11:16 Avery Chen: Console provides token-level usage with request metadata, timestamps, and response hashes; for Private deployments we can stream audit logs to your S3 or syslog with KMS encryption. we'll include an example schema.
11:30 Rina Sato: great. can we try a short sanity test in our staging VPC now? maybe run 5 concurrent clients sending short prompts and observe p50/p95/p99?
11:42 Avery Chen: yes let's schedule a 2 hour window next week and we'll bring a small infra change to route through an internal NLB and an interface endpoint. Daniel, Omar — can you pick a time?
11:52 Daniel Park: yes we'll propose Tuesday 10am PT.
11:55 Priya Patel: quick heads-up — during the pilot we'll enable sticky routing and debug logs for 30 minutes, then revert to normal to measure steady state.
12:05 Omar Rahman: one more networking nuance — our transit gateway has route propagation from multiple accounts. any guidance on route priorities?
12:12 Priya Patel: prefer explicit static routes for the service VPC destinations to avoid unexpected propagation. and tag route tables clearly; we've seen accidental route overrides in multi-team accounts.
12:24 Rina Sato: noted. also curious about soft-failover: if a worker can't be reached due to AZ outage do you have automatic model fallback?
12:33 Priya Patel: yes we have ring-based rollout policies and automatic fallback to a multi-AZ pool with a compatible variant; degrade gracefully to a slightly smaller model if needed.
12:43 Daniel Park: excellent — anything else we should record?
12:47 Avery Chen: action items recap: Priya shares KV tuning docs and runtime kernel tunables; Daniel shares route tables and security groups; Avery shares pricing and audit schema. we'll reconvene after pilot.
12:58 Rina Sato: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
13:03 Meeting end.
